posts.image_prompt: Archaeologists in 1930s clothing kneeling in a vast sandy trench on an English heath, the ghostly outline of a long wooden ship preserved only as neat rows of rusted iron nails in the sand, a woman in a long coat and hat watching from the edge, soft golden late-summer light, cinematic
posts.caption:
⚓ A SHIP BURIED UNDER AN ENGLISH FIELD

In the late 1930s, landowner Edith Pretty asked a self-taught local excavator named Basil Brown to dig into the mysterious mounds on her estate at Sutton Hoo, in Suffolk, England.

In 1939 he found something nobody expected: the outline of a ship more than 80 feet long. The wood had rotted away completely. Only its 'ghost' remained — rows of iron nails still sitting in the sand.

In the middle was a burial chamber full of treasure: a gold belt buckle, silver tableware from distant lands, and a full-face iron helmet unlike anything ever found in Britain.

But there was no body. Acidic soil may have dissolved it.

Most historians think this was the grave of Rædwald, King of East Anglia, who died around 624 AD. Nobody can prove it.

Edith Pretty donated the entire find to the British Museum.

Would you have given away a king's treasure found in your own garden?

posts.title: The explosion that left no crater

scenes.image_prompt: A blinding bluish fireball streaking across a pale morning sky above an endless Siberian pine forest, early 1900s, dramatic cinematic light
scenes.narration: In 1908, something exploded over Siberia and flattened a forest. It left no crater.

scenes.image_prompt: Aerial view of a remote Siberian taiga at dawn, rivers winding through dense dark green forest, mist, wide cinematic shot
scenes.narration: It happened on the morning of June thirtieth, nineteen-oh-eight, over a remote stretch of forest in Siberia, in the Russian Empire.

scenes.image_prompt: Vast expanse of millions of fallen pine trees lying in the same direction across rolling hills, flattened forest, overcast sky, photorealistic
scenes.narration: A blast in the sky knocked down an estimated eighty million trees across more than two thousand square kilometres. Windows broke hundreds of miles away.

scenes.narration: It took until nineteen twenty-seven for an expedition led by Leonid Kulik to reach the site. He found the devastation, but no crater and no meteorite.

scenes.narration: Today most scientists think an asteroid or comet exploded around five to ten kilometres up. The energy may have been about four megatons, hundreds of times the Hiroshima bomb.

scenes.narration: But exactly what it was is still debated. Asteroid or comet? Tell us in the comments, and follow for more.

posts.caption:
☄️ 80 million trees flattened. No crater. No meteorite.

On June 30, 1908, a blast over remote Siberia levelled around 2,150 square kilometres of forest. Scientists believe an asteroid or comet exploded in mid-air.

Rock or ice — which do you think it was? 👇

posts.image_prompt: A Norse warrior standing on a rocky Scandinavian shore beside a longship, wearing a simple rounded iron helmet with an eye-and-nose guard and no horns, wool tunic and round wooden shield on his back, misty fjord, cinematic natural light
posts.caption:
🪖 VIKINGS NEVER WORE HORNED HELMETS

It's one of history's most famous images — and it's wrong.

The most complete Viking helmet ever found was dug up at Gjermundbu, Norway, in 1943. It dates to the 10th century. It's a rounded iron cap with a guard for the eyes and nose. No horns.

So where did the horns come from? Largely from an opera.

For an 1876 production of Richard Wagner's 'Der Ring des Nibelungen', costume designer Carl Emil Doepler gave the Norse characters horned helmets. The look stuck — in paintings, cartoons and films.

Real fighters had good reason to skip them: horns could snag on branches or catch an enemy's blow.

What other 'fact' about the Vikings do you suspect is a myth?

posts.title: The receipts that burned down Parliament
posts.hook_text: ON THIS DAY: RECEIPTS BURNED PARLIAMENT

scenes.image_prompt: The medieval Palace of Westminster engulfed in towering orange flames at night, reflected in the River Thames, crowds silhouetted on a stone bridge, 1834 London
scenes.narration: Britain's Parliament was burned down by its own old receipts.

scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a bundle of notched wooden tally sticks, split hazel wood with carved notches, lying on a dusty table in a dim medieval counting house
scenes.narration: For centuries, the government recorded tax payments on notched wooden tally sticks.

scenes.image_prompt: A grand Georgian government office with clerks in 1820s coats stacking cartloads of old wooden sticks into a storeroom, candlelight
scenes.narration: The system was abolished in 1826. That left about two cartloads of old sticks sitting at the Palace of Westminster.

scenes.image_prompt: Two labourers in 1830s work clothes feeding bundles of wooden sticks into a glowing iron furnace in a cramped brick cellar
scenes.narration: On October 16, 1834, workers fed them into two furnaces under the House of Lords. Those furnaces were built for coal, not wood.

scenes.image_prompt: Smoke curling up through gaps in an ornate wooden floor of a Gothic chamber, a few visitors in 1830s dress looking down puzzled
scenes.narration: By afternoon, visitors felt heat rising through the floor. That evening, the woodwork caught fire.

scenes.image_prompt: A vast crowd in top hats and bonnets watching a blazing palace from the riverbank, a painter sketching on a small easel
scenes.narration: Thousands watched the palace burn. The painter J. M. W. Turner was so struck, he later painted the scene twice.

scenes.image_prompt: The ancient timber hammerbeam roof of Westminster Hall soaked with water, firemen with leather buckets and hand pumps protecting it amid smoke
scenes.narration: The twist? Firefighters saved medieval Westminster Hall. And from the ashes rose the Parliament building, Big Ben's tower included, that the world knows today.

scenes.image_prompt: The Gothic Revival Houses of Parliament and the clock tower at golden dusk, River Thames in the foreground, no people
scenes.narration: Was it carelessness, or just bad luck? Tell us below. Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🔥 ON THIS DAY in 1834, Britain's Parliament burned down — and the fuel was its own old tax receipts.

For centuries the Exchequer recorded payments on notched wooden tally sticks. After the system was scrapped in 1826, about two cartloads were left at the Palace of Westminster. Burning them in furnaces built for coal set the building alight.

Westminster Hall survived. The rest was rebuilt as the Parliament we know today.

Who do you blame: the workers, or the officials who gave the order? 👇
